card.chief_complaint: heavy legs and escalating mid-back pain

ask.changes_what: Positive: same-day whole-spine MRI (urgent if any neurological deficit) and dexamethasone per local pathway; negative: routine care unless other red flags accumulate.
ask.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for a neurological examination; do not let an absent cancer history delay imaging when there are motor, sensory or sphincter symptoms.
ask.escalation_warning: Back pain plus leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia or urinary retention in a cancer patient is metastatic cord compression until proven otherwise: emergency MRI and steroids.
ask.how: Ask specifically about any prior cancer diagnosis (including remote and 'cured'), and characterize the pain: onset, progression, night or rest pain, thoracic location, unexplained weight loss, and duration over one month. Then screen for cord/cauda equina symptoms: leg weakness, gait change, saddle numbness, urinary retention or incontinence.
ask.negative_finding: No cancer history makes spinal malignancy unlikely in primary care (prevalence <1%), but minor red flags (age >50, weight loss, failure to improve) are weakly informative and cannot exclude it.
ask.pitfalls: Age >50, night pain and weight loss have high false-positive rates when used alone. Sensitivity of 'history of cancer' is modest, so its absence does not clear a patient with progressive or thoracic pain.
ask.positive_finding: A prior cancer history is the only red flag shown to substantially raise the probability of spinal malignancy: post-test probability 7% in primary care and 33% in an ED cohort. With new neurological symptoms treat as possible metastatic cord compression.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable history or collateral; access to oncology records if the patient is unsure.
ask.title: New or progressive back pain in a patient with known cancer (or age >50, night pain, weight loss)

ask.changes_what: Positive: fingerstick now, treat, and observe for recurrence (sulfonylurea/renal failure -> admit); negative: keep glucose check but move to cardiac/neurologic causes of the spell.
ask.contraindications: None; the history must never delay a point-of-care glucose in any patient with altered mental status, syncope or focal deficit.
ask.do_not_use_when: Never rely on symptom history alone in an obtunded, post-ictal or focally weak patient - measure glucose immediately.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypoglycemia with sulfonylurea, insulin overdose, renal failure or alcohol needs monitored admission and repeated glucose; persistent deficit after glucose correction is a stroke workup.
ask.how: Ask specifically about insulin or sulfonylurea use (drug, dose, timing of last dose), missed or delayed meals, alcohol, recent renal or hepatic decline, and prodromal autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) or neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, difficulty speaking, weakness). Confirm with a fingerstick glucose at the time of symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure to insulin or secretagogues and no critical illness, cortisol/hormone deficiency or alcohol makes drug-induced hypoglycemia unlikely, but a measured glucose is still required because neuroglycopenia can present without warning symptoms.
ask.pitfalls: Long-standing diabetes and beta-blockers blunt autonomic warning symptoms so neuroglycopenic presentation (confusion, focal deficit) may be the only clue; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs for 24-72 h so a single corrected glucose is not the end of the episode.
ask.positive_finding: Insulin/secretagogue exposure plus a missed meal, alcohol or renal impairment and autonomic or neuroglycopenic prodrome makes hypoglycemia likely; Whipple's triad (symptoms, documented low glucose, resolution with glucose) confirms it.
ask.prerequisites: A collateral history when the patient is confused; the medication list including recently added sulfonylureas, insulin dose changes, or drugs that potentiate them.
ask.title: Hypoglycemia history: insulin/sulfonylurea use, missed meals, adrenergic or neuroglycopenic symptoms

ask.changes_what: Positive → CK, creatinine, potassium, urinalysis; start IV fluids; assess compartments. Negative → still send CK if found down, post-seizure or toxin-exposed.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not exclude rhabdomyolysis by history in obtunded, intoxicated or found-down patients — send CK.
ask.escalation_warning: Tense painful compartment, hyperkalemia or rising creatinine → urgent surgical and nephrology involvement.
ask.how: Ask about muscle pain, weakness, swelling and dark tea/cola-coloured urine, and exposures: found down/prolonged immobilization, seizure, extreme exertion or heat, crush or trauma, cocaine/amphetamines, alcohol, statins/fibrates, antipsychotics (NMS), recent infection. Palpate for tender, swollen or tense muscle compartments and check distal pulses and sensation.
ask.negative_finding: Absent muscle symptoms or dark urine do not exclude rhabdomyolysis; many cases are oligosymptomatic and even qualitative urine myoglobin was positive in only 19% of 475 inpatients (PMID 16267412, Abstract). Measure CK whenever risk factors exist.
ask.pitfalls: Dark urine also comes from hematuria, hemoglobinuria or bilirubin. In 60% of cases multiple causes co-exist and toxins account for 46% (PMID 16267412, Abstract); CK peaks at 24–72 h, so an early value may be modest (unverified recall).
ask.positive_finding: Myalgia or weakness with dark urine after immobilization, exertion, seizure or toxin exposure strongly suggests rhabdomyolysis; check CK and a urine dipstick (heme-positive without red cells).
ask.prerequisites: Collateral history for obtunded or intoxicated patients; medication and drug-use review.
ask.title: Muscle pain/weakness, prolonged immobilization or exertion, dark cola-colored urine

examine.changes_what: Positive: emergency MRI whole lumbosacral spine/urgent spinal surgical referral. Negative: does not exclude cauda equina; if suspicion persists (bilateral sciatica, retention) still image.
examine.contraindications: Patient refusal; rectal exam may be deferred if imaging is already being obtained emergently, but perineal sensation should still be tested.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use normal anal tone or perineal sensation to defer imaging when bilateral sciatica, new urinary retention or incontinence is present; the exam is insensitive for early cauda equina.
examine.escalation_warning: Any new saddle sensory change, sphincter disturbance or retention with back pain is a surgical emergency: emergent MRI and spinal referral without waiting for full deficit.
examine.how: With a chaperone and consent, test light touch and pinprick over the perineum, perianal skin, buttocks and inner thighs (S2-S5) comparing sides and asking about numbness when wiping; then digital rectal examination assessing resting anal tone, voluntary squeeze, and perianal sensation/anal wink. Pair with a bladder scan for post-void residual.
examine.negative_finding: Normal perineal sensation and anal tone do not exclude cauda equina compression - pooled sensitivities of individual red flags are only 0.19-0.43, and the diagnosis is often early or incomplete when sphincter signs are absent.
examine.pitfalls: Subjective perineal numbness is more sensitive than objective testing; anal tone is unreliable with prior anorectal surgery, chronic constipation or in the elderly. A large post-void residual (>500 mL) is the single most predictive bedside finding and should be checked with the exam.
examine.positive_finding: New saddle sensory loss or reduced anal tone in a patient with back pain and bilateral leg or sphincter symptoms is a red flag that mandates emergency MRI; pooled red flags for MRI-confirmed cauda equina are more specific (0.62-0.88) than sensitive.
examine.prerequisites: Chaperone, explanation and consent; document time of onset of bladder/bowel symptoms and bilateral leg symptoms.
examine.title: Saddle (perineal) sensory loss and reduced anal tone

examine.changes_what: Positive: emergency whole-spine MRI, dexamethasone if malignancy suspected, spinal/oncology referral. Negative in suspected GBS: pursue neuromuscular workup; retained UMN signs argue against GBS.
examine.contraindications: None; in acute spinal shock reflexes may be absent below the level for days, so hyporeflexia does not exclude cord compression.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on absent hyperreflexia or a normal plantar response to exclude acute cord compression, and do not delay imaging to complete a detailed sensory map.
examine.escalation_warning: New bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level, or new bladder dysfunction in a patient with known cancer is metastatic spinal cord compression until MRI proves otherwise; outcome depends on ambulatory status at treatment, so image within hours.
examine.how: Test pinprick and light touch moving upward from the feet on the trunk to find a dermatome above which sensation becomes normal; confirm with temperature (cold tuning fork). Test knee and ankle reflexes, clonus, and the plantar response by stroking the lateral sole from heel toward the toes with a blunt object; check bladder with a post-void residual.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of a sensory level or of upper motor neuron signs does not exclude early cord compression, because acute lesions can present with flaccidity and areflexia (spinal shock) and sensory levels are often imprecise; in GBS reflexes are lost and no level is found.
examine.pitfalls: The Babinski sign has only fair inter-rater reliability (kappa 0.30) and agreed with known upper motor neuron weakness in just 56% of examinations; withdrawal from a ticklish sole mimics an extensor response. The clinical level often lies several segments below the true lesion, so image the whole spine.
examine.positive_finding: A bilateral sensory level on the trunk with hyperreflexia, clonus, or extensor plantars below it localizes to the spinal cord and, with back pain in a patient with cancer, indicates metastatic cord compression until MRI proves otherwise.
examine.prerequisites: Cooperative patient able to report sensation; know dermatome landmarks (T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal); compare bilaterally.
examine.title: Sensory level with hyperreflexia / extensor plantar (Babinski) below the level

examine.changes_what: Positive: admit, serial FVC/single breath count, cardiac monitoring, LP and NCS, start IVIG/PLEX. Negative: check electrolytes and CK; image the spine if a sensory level or sphincter signs.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use preserved reflexes alone to dismiss GBS early in the course; do not use this pattern to exclude cord compression when back pain, a sensory level or sphincter change is present.
examine.escalation_warning: Dyspnea, weak cough, single breath count <20 or FVC <20 mL/kg, bulbar weakness or autonomic instability indicate impending respiratory failure: ICU-level monitoring.

evidence.citation: Fokke C, van den Berg B, Drenthen J, Walgaard C, van Doorn PA, Jacobs BC. Diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome and validation of Brighton criteria. Brain. 2014;137(1):33-43.
evidence.population: 494 adults with GBS previously enrolled in therapeutic and observational studies (Dutch cohorts); no non-GBS comparison group
evidence.quote: Decreased reflexes in paretic arms or legs were found initially in 91% of patients and in all patients during follow-up.
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of GBS by treating neurologists (trial/observational study inclusion)
evidence.target_condition: Guillain-Barre syndrome; finding = decreased reflexes in paretic limbs at initial examination

evidence.citation: Fokke C, van den Berg B, Drenthen J, Walgaard C, van Doorn PA, Jacobs BC. Diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome and validation of Brighton criteria. Brain. 2014;137(1):33-43.
evidence.population: Same cohort of 494 adults with GBS
evidence.quote: Disease nadir was reached within 2 weeks in 80%, within 4 weeks in 97% and within 6 weeks in all patients.
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of GBS (trial/observational study inclusion)
evidence.target_condition: Guillain-Barre syndrome; finding = bilateral limb weakness reaching nadir within 4 weeks

examine.how: Test proximal and distal strength in all four limbs (MRC grading), compare sides, and elicit biceps, triceps, knee and ankle reflexes with reinforcement. Ask about onset and progression (hours to days, distal to proximal), preceding diarrhea or respiratory illness within 4 weeks, sensory symptoms, facial or bulbar weakness, and back pain or sphincter change.
examine.negative_finding: Preserved brisk reflexes, a sensory level, early sphincter dysfunction, marked asymmetry or fever at onset point toward myelopathy, cord compression or other mimics; however 2% of GBS patients keep normal reflexes in paretic arms.
examine.pitfalls: Reflexes may be normal on day 1 and lost later, so re-examine; hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia and myopathy produce symmetric weakness with preserved reflexes. Weakness stayed leg-restricted in 6% and arm-restricted in 1%.
examine.positive_finding: Bilateral, relatively symmetric, progressive flaccid weakness with reduced or absent reflexes in the weak limbs, reaching nadir within 4 weeks, is the Brighton level-1 to 3 clinical core of GBS; 91% of GBS patients have decreased reflexes at presentation.
examine.prerequisites: Cooperative patient; reflex hammer; document time course and check bedside respiratory measures (single breath count / FVC) at the same visit.
examine.title: Ascending symmetric limb weakness with absent/reduced reflexes (after recent GI/URI illness)

examine.changes_what: Positive: activate stroke pathway/immediate imaging and time-critical reperfusion assessment. Negative: lowers probability but still image if dizziness, ataxia or visual symptoms.
examine.contraindications: None; if the patient cannot cooperate, observe spontaneous facial symmetry and limb movement instead.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative screen to exclude posterior-circulation stroke in a patient with acute dizziness, ataxia, diplopia or visual field loss; use HINTS/gait assessment and imaging pathways instead.
examine.escalation_warning: Any positive item with symptom onset within the reperfusion window is a time-critical emergency; do not delay activation for a glucose result unless hypoglycemia is confirmed and deficits resolve with correction.

evidence.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
evidence.population: Pooled studies of patients with suspected stroke evaluated with modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
evidence.quote: LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1 ... LR of 0 findings = 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25-0.61
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and relevant laboratory tests
evidence.target_condition: Acute stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) among patients with neurologically relevant symptoms

evidence.citation: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.
evidence.population: Convenience sample of 171 ED and neurology inpatients, 49 with stroke/TIA
evidence.quote: abnormality in any 1 of the 3 stroke scale items had a sensitivity of 66% and specificity of 87% in identifying a stroke patient.
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke or TIA
evidence.target_condition: Stroke or TIA (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal, scored by physician)

evidence.citation: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.
evidence.population: Same 171-patient convenience sample; subgroup with anterior circulation stroke
evidence.quote: The sensitivity was 88% for identification of patients with anterior circulation strokes.
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke, anterior circulation
evidence.target_condition: Anterior circulation stroke (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal)

examine.how: Ask the patient to smile or show teeth and look for asymmetric facial movement; have them close eyes and hold both arms out palms-up for 10 seconds, watching for one arm drifting down; ask them to repeat a simple sentence and listen for slurring, wrong words, or inability to speak. Any one abnormal item is a positive screen.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of all three findings lowers but does not exclude stroke (LR about 0.4); posterior-circulation strokes, which often present with dizziness or ataxia, are commonly missed by this screen (Kothari: 66% sensitivity overall vs 88% for anterior circulation).
examine.pitfalls: Bell palsy, old deficits, intoxication, hypoglycemia and seizure mimics all produce false positives; isolated vertigo, ataxia, visual field loss and neglect are not captured, so a negative screen must not stop a stroke work-up in a dizzy patient.
examine.positive_finding: Any new facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech; in patients with neurologically relevant symptoms this raises the probability of stroke (pooled LR about 5.5).
examine.prerequisites: Patient awake enough to follow simple commands; check a fingerstick glucose alongside the screen. Note time last known well.
examine.title: Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech (Cincinnati/FAST screen)
